title: MASTER_KEY → AES-256 key derivation is a single unsalted SHA-256 round (no KDF iterations); dictionary-strength env passphrase + stolen DB = offline bulk decrypt of every provider API key
evidence: crypto.go:21-23 — `func NewCipher(masterKey string) (*Cipher, error) {` / `sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(masterKey))` / `block, err := aes.NewCipher(sum[:])`. The env value is accepted verbatim with no minimum length/entropy check (config.go:64 `MasterKey: getenv("MASTER_KEY", "llm-router-guard-master-key"),`), and every provider key is sealed under this one derived key (providers.go:64 `enc, err := s.enc.Encrypt(req.APIKey)`, stored in providers.api_key_enc, model.go:107).
impact: A single SHA-256 per candidate is GPU-crackable at billions of guesses/sec. If gateway.db (or a MySQL/PG dump) is exfiltrated and the operator chose a human-chosen MASTER_KEY (the code and .env.template actively encourage copy-paste of the shipped default), all upstream provider API keys (OpenAI/Anthropic billing accounts) are decrypted offline. The warn-only default check (main.go:191-193) only fires for the exact literal default, not for weak-but-custom values — this is the NEW consequence beyond the stated 'warn-only defaults' fact.
recommendation: Derive the cipher key with a memory-hard, iterated KDF (Argon2id or scrypt; PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 ≥600k iterations as a floor) using a random salt stored alongside the ciphertext header; enforce a minimum MASTER_KEY entropy at startup (e.g., reject <20 chars or non-random). Provide a re-encrypt/rotation tool so MASTER_KEY can actually be changed (today main.go:192 tells operators rotation requires manual re-entry of every provider key).
mitigations_checked: AES-GCM itself is correct: 12-byte random nonce per Encrypt call from crypto/rand (crypto.go:34-40), nonce prepended, auth tag verified on Decrypt (crypto.go:52). Ciphertext (not plaintext) is what is stored. Nonce-reuse risk is negligible at this message volume. No AAD binding to provider ID (tamper-within-DB swap of ciphertexts between rows is possible but requires DB write access).

title: World-known default admin credentials admin/admin123 baked into every first-boot path (code, docker-compose, .env.template) with no forced change on first login
evidence: main.go:170-173 — `pass := cfg.AdminPassword` / `if pass == "" {` / `pass = "admin123" // 仅在未设置环境变量时默认，首次启动后必须修改` / `log.Println("[bootstrap] WARNING: using default admin password 'admin123'. Set ADMIN_PASSWORD to change.")`. Reinforced by docker-compose.yml:18 `- ADMIN_PASSWORD=${ADMIN_PASSWORD:-admin123}` and the tracked template .env.template:28 `ADMIN_PASSWORD=admin123`. issueLogin (auth.go:133-138) only ever nudges MFA binding (`needBind := sec.MFAEnabled && sec.MFARequiredAll && !u.MFAEnabled`) — there is no must-change-password flag anywhere.
impact: This is a distinct default from the already-disclosed JWT_SECRET/MASTER_KEY warn-only pair: it grants direct unauthenticated → full admin (all provider keys re-enterable/exportable via testProvider, all gateway keys creatable) on any deployment that follows the documented `cp .env.template .env` + `docker compose up` path without editing line 28. A single console login endpoint (routes.go:42 `api.POST("/auth/login", s.login)`) exposed on a routable interface is trivially owned by scripted credential stuffing of the values printed in the project's own template.
recommendation: Remove the literal from .env.template and docker-compose (use `${ADMIN_PASSWORD:?set admin password}` like the redis service already does at docker-compose.yml:37); on bootstrap-without-env, generate a random password, print it once, and/or set a must_change_password flag enforced in middleware until changePassword runs.
mitigations_checked: Login does apply bcrypt + 5-fail/15-min lockout (auth.go:76, 113-122), so online guessing of a *changed* password is throttled; bootstrap only runs when admin_users is empty (main.go:166-168). None of these help against the known default itself.

title: Config rollback / backup-restore silently destroys all provider API key material: bundle claims to keep ciphertext but APIKeyEnc is json:"-" and RestoreBundle deletes+reinserts providers with empty keys
evidence: bundle.go:15-17 — `// ConfigBundle 可序列化的全量配置（密钥保持 DB 原样密文，跨版本/备份一致）。` / `type ConfigBundle struct {` / `Providers  []model.Provider`. But model.go:107 — `APIKeyEnc    string    `gorm:"type:text" json:"-"` // AES-GCM 加密存储 (REQ-005 ④)` — so `json.Marshal(b)` (backup.go:31 `body, _ := json.Marshal(b)`; manager.go:386 `if b, err := json.Marshal(bundle); err == nil {`) omits the ciphertext entirely. RestoreBundle then hard-clears and recreates: bundle.go:82 `&model.Provider{}, &model.AliasUpstream{}, ...` → bundle.go:86 `tx.Where("1 = 1").Delete(table)` → bundle.go:91 `tx.Create(&b.Providers)` with APIKeyEnc="". Reload maps that to an empty live key: manager.go:218 `p.APIKey = "" // 解密失败：保留空密钥，该上游调用时会失败`.
impact: Every POST /config/rollback (routes.go:139) and POST /backups/restore (routes.go:147) irreversibly wipes all provider credentials (all historical ConfigVersion snapshots are equally key-less, so there is no recovery path), taking the whole gateway down with upstream 401s and forcing manual re-entry of every vendor key — the disaster-recovery feature is the disaster. Conversely, the same tag means backups/exports leak nothing, so this is integrity/availability, not confidentiality.
recommendation: Either serialize the ciphertext in the bundle (explicit field with its own marshal tag, e.g. `api_key_enc_b64`, since it is already encrypted at rest) or refuse to delete/recreate providers whose key material is absent from the bundle; fail loudly instead of silently loading empty keys.
mitigations_checked: Plaintext never enters the bundle: model.Provider.APIKey is `gorm:"-" json:"-"` (model.go:108) and is only populated in the in-memory snapshot (manager.go:215). BackupRecord.Content is `json:"-"` (model.go:290) so createBackup's response (backup.go:42 `s.ok(c, rec)`) does not echo the bundle. ConfigBundle has no AdminUser field (bundle.go:16-27), so password hashes, MFASecret and RecoveryCodesJSON are NOT in backups/exports — checklist item confirmed clean.

title: TOTP secrets stored in plaintext in the database (and pending setup secrets in Redis with optional auth), unlike provider keys which are encrypted — DB/Redis read = second factor bypass
evidence: model.go:17 — `MFASecret         string     `gorm:"size:128" json:"-"` // TOTP base32 secret（未启用也暂存，待 enable）`. Persisted verbatim at enable: auth.go:243-246 — `s.db.Model(&model.AdminUser{}).Where("id = ?", uid).Updates(map[string]any{` / `"mfa_secret": secret, "mfa_enabled": true, "mfa_bound_at": &now,`. Multi-node schemas confirm plaintext columns: deploy/schema/schema.postgres.sql:33 `mfa_secret character varying(128),` and deploy/schema/schema.mysql.sql:29 `` `mfa_secret` varchar(128) COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci DEFAULT NULL,``. Pending secrets also sit plaintext in Redis: redis_mfa.go:111 `r.rdb.Set(ctx, r.setupKey(uid), secret, mfaTicketTTL)` with password optional (docker-compose.yml:22 `- REDIS_PASSWORD=${REDIS_PASSWORD:-}`).
impact: The project already treats at-rest confidentiality of secrets as important enough to AES-GCM provider keys, but the second factor is stored raw. Anyone who reads the DB file (gateway.db is a single copyable file, config.go:62), a SQL dump, a backup pipeline, or an unauthenticated shared Redis obtains live TOTP seeds; combined with the bcrypt password hash (or the admin123 default) this is complete, persistent account takeover of every MFA-enabled admin — MFA becomes decorative against exactly the theft scenario it exists for.
recommendation: Encrypt MFASecret with the existing s.enc (same pattern as Provider.APIKeyEnc), or at minimum document that DB file/backup protection is a 2FA-boundary requirement. Require REDIS_PASSWORD (or TLS/ACLs) whenever REDIS_ADDR is set.
mitigations_checked: MFASecret/RecoveryCodesJSON/PasswordHash are `json:"-"` so they never appear in API responses (listUsers builds a sanitized userRow, users.go:10-34), in op-logs (audit.LogOp marshals via encoding/json, audit.go:110-119), or in backups (no AdminUser in ConfigBundle). Recovery codes are stored as SHA-256 hashes of 64-bit-random codes (mfa.go:47 `p := crypto.RandomHex(8)`, mfa.go:50 `hashed[i] = crypto.Sha256Hex(p)`) — unsalted SHA-256 is acceptable here because 2^64 entropy defeats offline reversal; codes are single-use via Pop-style consumption (mfa.go:61-76).

title: Admin JWTs are unrevocable for 24h: logout is a no-op, and neither password change nor forced MFA unbind invalidates already-issued tokens
evidence: jwt.go:20-24 — `RegisteredClaims: jwt.RegisteredClaims{` / `ExpiresAt: jwt.NewNumericDate(time.Now().Add(24 * time.Hour)),` — no jti, and no denylist exists anywhere (grep: only Parse in middleware.go:23 and auditws.go:31). Logout discards nothing server-side: auth.go:152-155 — `func (s *Server) logout(c *gin.Context) {` / `s.recordOp(c, "login", "auth", "logout", nil, nil)` / `s.ok(c, nil)`. changePassword (auth.go:180-181) and admin-side unbindUserMfa (users.go:48-49) update only the DB row.
impact: The documented incident-response sequence (change password / unbind attacker-enrolled MFA / 'log out' everywhere) does not evict an attacker: a stolen token (localStorage XSS, the ?token= query-string copy used by the audit WebSocket, routes.go:116-118 + auditws.go:31 `auth.Parse(s.secret, c.Query("token"))`) keeps full admin — including creating API keys and reading provider keys via testProvider — for up to 24 hours after the owner believes they rotated credentials. This is a NEW consequence beyond the stated 'JWT HS256' fact.
recommendation: Add a per-user token epoch (e.g., `pwd_changed_at`/`token_ver` claim checked in AuthMiddleware, bumped by changePassword, unbind, unlock) and/or a short-lived access token with refresh; prefer cookie/header auth for the WebSocket instead of query-string tokens.
mitigations_checked: Claims are minimal (uid/uname/iss/iat/exp, jwt.go:11-15) — no secrets in the payload; HMAC-only method is pinned (jwt.go:31-34 rejects non-HMAC, blocking alg-confusion); 24h expiry bounds the window; server access log records only URL.Path (main.go:109,116), so the WS ?token= is not logged by the app itself.

title: Hardcoded credentials committed to the repository in tracked deploy/ scripts (MySQL/Postgres/Redis password 'comeback', E2E admin password, JWT/MASTER keys)
evidence: deploy/env.sh:3-6 — `export DB_MYSQL_DSN='root:comeback@tcp(127.0.0.1:3306)/gateway_mysql?charset=utf8mb4&parseTime=True&loc=Local'` / `export DB_PG_DSN='host=127.0.0.1 port=5432 user=postgres password=comeback dbname=gateway_pg sslmode=disable TimeZone=Asia/Shanghai'` / `export MYSQL_PWD=comeback` / `export PGPASSWORD=comeback`. deploy/run_server.sh:13-14 — `JWT_SECRET="e2e-jwt-secret-2026" MASTER_KEY="e2e-master-key-2026" \` / `ADMIN_PASSWORD="E2eAdmin#2026" GIN_MODE=release \`. Also verify_schema.sh:16-17,33-39, make_schema.sh:16,24, mn_circuit.sh:12, mn_redis.sh:20-22 (`REDIS_PASSWORD=comeback`). `git ls-files` confirms all of these are tracked (deploy/llm-router-guard-linux-amd64 exists on disk but is correctly ignored via .gitignore:27).
impact: In an open-source repo these values are permanently in VCS history and serve as copy-paste material for real deployments; the same dictionary password guards MySQL root, Postgres superuser and Redis in the multi-node test topology, and the committed MASTER_KEY/JWT_SECRET pattern normalizes putting the two most sensitive env vars in shell scripts. Anyone with repo read access learns the exact bootstrap credentials of any environment started with these scripts (run_server.sh binds a real admin login 'E2eAdmin#2026' that testers reuse).
recommendation: Move secrets to an untracked env file (the .gitignore:8 `.env` pattern already covers it), rotate the 'comeback'/'E2eAdmin#2026' credentials, and scrub history (git filter-repo) if the repo is or becomes public.
mitigations_checked: All DSNs point at 127.0.0.1 (loopback test instances), so remote exploitation of these exact credentials is unlikely; .gitignore:6-8 correctly ignores `gateway.db*`, `data/`, `.env` — verified via git ls-files that no .db/.env is tracked (gateway.db, gateway.db-wal, gateway.db-shm exist on disk only, untracked).

title: Unredacted upstream error bodies are echoed to gateway clients, admin responses and audit rows — vendor auth failures characteristically embed fragments of the provider API key
evidence: gateway.go:539-543 — `ap.errMsg = msg` / `ap.status = "error"` / `clientError(c, clientProto, resp.StatusCode,` / `fmt.Sprintf("upstream returned %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, msg),` where msg = `adapter.ExtractError(up.Protocol, body)` (gateway.go:531) from the provider's error body. OpenAI/Anthropic 401 bodies embed key prefix+suffix (e.g. 'Incorrect API key provided: sk-abc…xyz123'). Same echo on the admin side: providers.go:198 — `ok, msg = false, "认证失败（API Key 无效或无权限）"+errSnippet(body)` (errSnippet takes up to 120 chars, providers.go:361-378), and the string is persisted to SLB state surfaced at dashboard.go:122 `"fail_count": h.FailCount, "last_error": h.LastError})` and to CallLog.ErrorMsg (model.go:266 `ErrorMsg string `gorm:"size:512" json:"error_msg"``, fed by gateway.go:539) which is listed/exported via /audit/calls.
impact: A low-privilege gateway API-key holder can receive fragments of the *provider-side* key (first ~8 + last ~4 chars) in a passthrough 4xx whenever upstream auth breaks — beyond what api_key_masked (front4+back2) already discloses to admins, and it is then stored in audit rows readable by every admin. Requires the stored key to be invalid/expired, so exposure is partial and situational — hence low.
recommendation: Redact upstream error messages before echoing/persisting: strip any `sk-[A-Za-z0-9._-]{8,}` pattern and cap length; keep full text server-side only in a debug channel.
mitigations_checked: No code path returns the stored plaintext key itself: create/update zero APIKeyEnc before responding (providers.go:81,130), list relies on `json:"-"` (model.go:107), testProvider/importProviderModels return only status text and model IDs (providers.go:218,356-357), and the one-time plaintext returns are limited to createApiKey (apikeys.go:54) and mfaEnable recovery codes (auth.go:248). The faithful-passthrough design decision was weighed; only the key-fragment echo is flagged.

title: bcrypt at DefaultCost(10) for admin password hashes, and GenerateFromPassword error ignored in changePassword
evidence: auth.go:180-181 — `hash, _ := bcrypt.GenerateFromPassword([]byte(req.NewPassword), bcrypt.DefaultCost)` / `s.db.Model(&model.AdminUser{}).Where("id = ?", uid).Update("password_hash", string(hash))`; same cost at bootstrap: main.go:175 `hash, err := bcrypt.GenerateFromPassword([]byte(pass), bcrypt.DefaultCost)`. bcrypt.DefaultCost = 10.
impact: Cost 10 is below current OWASP guidance (≥12 for bcrypt): offline cracking of a stolen admin_users table (already plaintext-MFASecret per secrets-4) is ~4x cheaper than cost 12 per doubling, compounding the DB-theft chain. The ignored error in changePassword would, on any GenerateFromPassword failure, write an empty password_hash (self-lockout, not bypass — CompareHashAndPassword always fails on a malformed hash, auth.go:176).
recommendation: Use bcrypt.Cost(12+) (or argon2id), check the error from GenerateFromPassword before updating, and consider a password strength policy beyond the current ≥8-char rule (auth.go:166-169).
mitigations_checked: CompareHashAndPassword used correctly on both login paths (auth.go:76,176); salted per-hash by bcrypt; online guessing throttled by 5-fail/15-min lockout (auth.go:113-122); PasswordHash is `json:"-"` (model.go:16) so it never appears in responses or op-logs.

title: MaskKey discards only 6 characters (front4+back2) and is collision-prone for display; ~12 bits of key material leaked per masked value
evidence: crypto.go:60-66 — `func MaskKey(s string) string {` / `r := []rune(s)` / `if len(r) <= 8 {` / `return "****"` / `}` / `return string(r[:4]) + "****" + string(r[len(r)-2:])`. Applied to gateway keys (apikeys.go:41 `KeyMasked: crypto.MaskKey(key),` — for 'sk-'+32hex this reveals 'sk-X' + last 2 hex chars ≈ 12 bits) and provider keys (providers.go:70 `APIKeyMasked: crypto.MaskKey(req.APIKey)` — for 'sk-proj-…' style keys the first 4 chars are a constant prefix, leaking only the last 2 chars).
impact: Masked values are stored (model.go:38,109) and shown in every list response; many vendors' keys share prefixes, so masks collide and the residual entropy (last 2 chars) is a small but real accelerator for any future partial-key disclosure. Not used in any authentication decision, so no bypass.
recommendation: Use a fixed-length suffix-only mask (e.g., last 4 chars) or a per-key short-ID column for disambiguation; keep the prefix out of the mask for known-constant prefixes.
mitigations_checked: Gateway auth compares full SHA-256 hashes via exact map lookup (gateway.go:215 `rec, ok := snap.APIKeys[crypto.Sha256Hex(key)]`, runtime/manager.go:272), never the mask; KeyHash is `json:"-"` (model.go:37) so list/update/export responses (apikeys.go:24,87) never leak the hash either.

title: In-memory MFA store ignores its own documented 5-minute TTL: login tickets and pending TOTP setup secrets live for the process lifetime
evidence: Header comment redis_mfa.go:21-22 — `// 票据（login ticket）与绑定密钥（setup secret）是短时效（5 分钟）一次性数据，` / `// 原实现在实例内存（sync.Map）…` and line 22 `// TTL 统一 5 分钟，替代原内存实现的 expiry 检查。` — but the mem implementation has no expiry at all: redis_mfa.go:37 `func (m *memMFA) SaveLoginTicket(token string, uid uint) { m.login.Store(token, uid) }` and redis_mfa.go:45 `func (m *memMFA) SaveSetupSecret(uid uint, secret string) { m.setup.Store(uid, secret) }`. Only redisMFA applies mfaTicketTTL (redis_mfa.go:93,111).
impact: On the default single-node (SQLite) deployment, a second-factor login ticket (auth.go:88-90 `token := crypto.RandomHex(16)` / `s.mfa().SaveLoginTicket(token, u.ID)`) and an unconfirmed TOTP secret (auth.go:220 `s.mfa().SaveSetupSecret(uid, secret)`) never expire until consumed — a setup secret captured from a memory dump or a leaked response stays valid indefinitely, and abandoned entries accumulate unbounded in the sync.Maps.
recommendation: Store (value, expiry) in memMFA and purge on Pop plus a periodic sweep, matching the Redis path's 5-minute semantics.
mitigations_checked: Tickets are 128-bit random and single-use via LoadAndDelete (redis_mfa.go:39,47); PopLoginTicket binds the ticket to its user ID (auth.go:52-55); tickets are only minted after a successful bcrypt password check (auth.go:76-91), so unauthenticated attackers cannot mint them; Redis path uses atomic GETDEL-equivalent luaPop (redis_mfa.go:59-65).
